text:
liam: Quick follow-up after the RFC review: we need to choose between offload-hint (implicit) and explicit-token offload for the allocator. Putting notes here so the runtime folks can weigh in.

sana: Thanks. can you sketch the runtime-visible differences in two lines?

liam: Sure. implicit: app marks pages with HINT_FOLD and runtime migrates based on pressure/latency heuristics. explicit: app calls offload(ptr) -> offload_token and manages restores.

jorge: Primary operational concern: implicit hides latency spikes. If we migrate synchronously due to a cache miss, request threads can stall unexpectedly. Explicit gives predictable behavior at the cost of more API surface.

liam: Agreed. Another angle: fragmentation + memcpy efficiency. With explicit slab-level offload we can move big contiguous ranges (good for PCIe throughput). With implicit pagefold we often move many small pages which kills throughput.

sana: Do we have numbers? Jorge did a micro last week, right?

jorge: Yep. Summary: single 256B page copy ~35us, 4k ~120us, 64k ~1.1ms. Per-byte cost decreases for larger transfers. Small transfers are ~8-12x more expensive per-byte. So fragmentation directly increases token cost.

liam: That's the key: fragmentation multiplies PCIe overhead and kernel memcpy syscall overhead. We should aim to preserve coalesced ranges when possible.

ops-bot: telemetry.job: offload-metrics-pilot started; sample_id=pilot-42

sana: Proposal: hybrid allocator modes. Allocator creation gets OFFLOAD_MODE = "explicit" | "hinted". Default explicit for model artifacts and kv-cache; hinted for ephemeral guest allocations.

jorge: Hybrid is reasonable. Runtime implications: we must implement two codepaths. For explicit we maintain a token table and evict by slab cohort. For hinted we run page-level eviction with a lightweight compaction pass that opportunistically coalesces adjacent resident pages before restoring.

liam: We also need stable identifiers for async restores. If compaction can move an object, callers must hold an offload_token, not raw ptr. Suggest API:
```c
offload_token_t offload(void* ptr); // returns token, frees GPU residency
int restore_async(offload_token_t t, restore_handle_t* out); // queues restore
int poll_restore(restore_handle_t h, void** out_ptr);
int restore_sync(offload_token_t t, void** out_ptr);
```
This lets callers avoid blocking and lets runtime coalesce restores for efficiency.

ops-bot: quota.enforce: pilot-42 tenant=team-x quota=8MB_async_restore_active

sana: Quotas: per-tenant async restore slots + per-tenant host staging bytes. If tenant exceeds staging bytes, reject new offloads with ENOSPC or fallback to compaction/compression.

jorge: Rejection semantics: better to fail fast with ENOSPC than to silently degrade latency. But we should offer graceful fallback: try compression (lossless or quantized) or queue with backpressure signal to requestor.

liam: For SDK ergonomics we should expose both sync and async paths. JS/Python default to async restore with awaitable handle; sync restore kept for convenience but documented as expensive.

ops-bot: telemetry: pilot-42 metrics: offloads=92, async_restores=41, avg_coalesced_bytes=48KB, 95p_restore_latency=240ms

sana: Telemetry items we should collect: offload_count per-type, avg_fragment_size histogram, coalesced_bytes_per_restore, memcpy_calls_per_restore, restore_latency p50/p95, rejected_offloads_by_reason. These inform slab size choices.

jorge: Also track "restore_efficiency" = coalesced_bytes / memcpy_calls (higher is better). If efficiency drops below threshold, trigger compaction tuning or raise slab_size.

liam: Edge cases: concurrent compaction + in-flight restore. Design: token -> allocation-id mapping that survives compaction. Compaction updates mapping atomically; restore_handle refers to allocation-id. If compaction moved the object, poll_restore resolves to new ptr.

ops-bot: build.check: allocator-token-mapping unit tests passed in canary build

sana: Action items: liam to write RFC addendum with the API and hybrid mode; jorge to add microbench scripts and baseline numbers; runtime team to start async-restore queue and token table; infra to add the telemetry metrics. Target: draft before next Thurs.

jorge: minor note: when we coalesce for restore, prefer contiguous slabs within the same NUMA locality to avoid extra host memcpy hops.

liam: Good call. I'll include a short canary plan: enable hybrid on canary pool, inject synthetic small-page fragmentation, measure restore_efficiency and tenant QoS. If numbers look bad we revert.

ops-bot: telemetry.job: pilot-42 snapshot saved as s3://redwood-canary/pilot-42/snapshot-2026-03-21

sana: thanks all. leaving this thread open for comments. if anyone thinks implicit-first (hinted-only) is better, please explain how we avoid the memcpy cliff and tenant noise.

jorge: I prefer explicit-first for kvcache/weights, hinted-only for best-effort guest memory. Hybrid is the pragmatic compromise.

liam: Agree. I'll file the addendum and ping reviewers.
